subject: Reasoning
description: Step-wise rearrangement, alphabetical/numerical sorting, two-rule alternation

questions.stem: Input: 25 pen 14 cap 36 box 9. Each step shifts the smallest available number to the leftmost position (then the smallest word alphabetically next, alternating). Step I would be:
questions.explanation: Rule alternates: Step I picks the SMALLEST NUMBER (9) and moves it to the leftmost position. Numbers 25, 14, 36, 9 → smallest = 9. Move 9 to the left: '9 25 pen 14 cap 36 box'. Step II would pick the smallest WORD alphabetically — 'box', and move it after the already-shifted number block. Each subsequent step alternates.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Input: 56 23 87 12 49 33. Each step moves the LARGEST number to the rightmost end. After Step II the arrangement is:
questions.explanation: Step I: move the largest (87) to the right end. Take it out and shift others left. Input: 56 23 87 12 49 33 → Step I: 56 23 12 49 33 87. Step II: move the next largest (56) to the rightmost-but-before-87 position → 23 12 49 33 56 87. So Step II = 23 12 49 33 56 87. Continuing: Step III moves 49 → 23 12 33 49 56 87; Step IV moves 33 → 23 12 33 49 56 87 (stable, sorted).

questions.stem: Input: cat dog ant bear elephant. Each step moves the alphabetically FIRST word to the leftmost position (already in the front then the next-first to the left of it). Step I:

options.option_text: cat dog ant bear elephant (no change)
ant bear cat dog elephant (fully sorted)

questions.explanation: Alphabetical order of given words: ant, bear, cat, dog, elephant. Step I — pick the alphabetically first ('ant') and move it to the leftmost position. Result: ant cat dog bear elephant. Step II would then move 'bear' next: ant bear cat dog elephant (now sorted). Each step processes ONE element.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: Input: 73 ape 41 bird 28 cat 65. The machine shifts the SMALLEST number to the right and alphabetically LAST word to the left, alternating (number first). Step I:
questions.explanation: Step I: numbers in input — 73, 41, 28, 65; smallest = 28. Move 28 to the rightmost position. Original: 73 ape 41 bird 28 cat 65. After Step I: 73 ape 41 bird cat 65 28. Step II would then move alphabetically last word ('cat' is currently last alphabetically among 'ape', 'bird', 'cat') to the LEFT end: cat 73 ape 41 bird 65 28.

questions.stem: If the machine fully sorts numbers in ASCENDING order from left to right, and the input is 88 15 47 22 63 31 — how many STEPS will the machine take to fully sort it (one number moved per step)?

options.option_text: 5 (n − 1 steps for n = 6 numbers; the last sorts itself)

questions.explanation: Machine input-output sorting typically takes (n − 1) steps when one element is fixed per step (selection-sort style). For n = 6 numbers → 5 steps. Verification (largest goes to right each step): Step I: 15 47 22 63 31 88; Step II: 15 47 22 31 63 88; Step III: 15 47 22 31 63 88 (no, 47 still > 22 → 15 22 47 31 63 88); Step IV: 15 22 31 47 63 88; Step V: stable. Generally 5 steps suffice. The (n−1) rule holds for any input of n distinct elements.

questions.stem: Input: hat 11 jam 4 kite 7 lily 19. Step rule: move the smallest number, then the next smallest, alternately preceded by their adjacent words, to the right end. The FINAL fully-sorted output (numbers ascending at right, words alphabetical at left) is:
questions.explanation: Final sorted output: words alphabetically (hat, jam, kite, lily) on the left + numbers ascending (4, 7, 11, 19) on the right. Words: h < j < k < l → hat jam kite lily. Numbers: 4 < 7 < 11 < 19. Result: 'hat jam kite lily 4 7 11 19'.
questions.subject: Reasoning

questions.stem: When solving machine input-output problems, the BEST strategy is to:

options.option_text: Identify the rule pattern by comparing two consecutive steps; the difference reveals the operation

questions.explanation: Method: (1) Compare Step (n) with Step (n+1) — only ONE element changes position per step in classical IO problems; (2) Identify what kind of element it is (smallest/largest number, alphabetically first/last word); (3) Identify where it moves (leftmost / rightmost / specific position relative to anchor); (4) Project forward to find the asked step or final output. Common rule patterns: bubble-sort numbers/words; alternating number-word; swap pairs; reverse halves. Speed comes from quickly spotting the rule from one transition.
